title: Justice Department Ruling Strips DACA Shield in Deportation Cases, Putting 500,000 Dreamers at Greater Risk
excerpt: A Board of Immigration Appeals decision bars immigration judges from dismissing removal proceedings solely because a respondent holds DACA status, in what advocates call a quiet rollback of protections.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The Board of Immigration Appeals ruling weakens DACA protections against deportation.
  • Over 505,000 DACA recipients are now at increased risk of removal.
  • In 2025, 261 DACA holders were arrested, with 86 deported.
  • The ruling reflects a broader strategy to undermine DACA without formal repeal.
  • DACA recipients face heightened vulnerability due to potential status lapses.

  • The Board of Immigration Appeals ruled that immigration judges cannot terminate removal proceedings solely because a respondent has been granted DACA — effectively stripping DACA of its de facto shield against deportation in court.
  • Approximately 505,000 DACA recipients are affected; between January and November 2025, 261 DACA holders were arrested and 86 removed from the country.
  • The ruling does not end DACA itself but makes it significantly easier for the government to pursue deportation cases against recipients who are in removal proceedings.
  • Advocates say the decision is part of a systematic effort to dismantle the program without formally rescinding it.

A Quiet Legal Shift

A precedential ruling by the Board of Immigration Appeals has removed one of the last practical shields protecting DACA recipients from deportation, in what immigration advocates describe as a backdoor dismantling of the program without the political cost of formally ending it.

In the case known as Santiago-Santiago (29 I&N Dec. 589), the BIA — the Justice Department body that sets binding precedent for all immigration courts — ruled that an immigration judge erred by terminating removal proceedings based solely on the fact that the respondent had been granted Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals. The decision means that holding DACA status alone is no longer sufficient grounds for a judge to dismiss a deportation case.

What Changed

Before this ruling, immigration judges in many jurisdictions would routinely close or terminate proceedings for respondents who held active DACA status, reasoning that the government had already determined these individuals were low-priority for removal. The practice was not universal, but it provided meaningful protection: if the government was not actively pursuing your deportation, judges saw little reason to keep the case alive.

The BIA's decision changes that calculus. Immigration judges must now consider DHS's stated reasons for opposing termination, even when the respondent holds valid DACA. In practical terms, this means DHS attorneys can keep deportation cases open against DACA holders indefinitely — and can move to deport them if their DACA status lapses or is revoked.

"This decision is yet another step in dismantling the program without the government taking responsibility for ending it outright. This is a quiet rollback of protections, and our communities are paying the price in real time."

— Juliana Macedo do Nascimento, United We Dream

The Numbers Behind the Threat

DACA, created by the Obama administration in 2012, currently protects approximately 505,000 people who were brought to the United States as children before 2007. Recipients must renew their status every two years, maintain clean criminal records, and meet educational requirements.

The program has always been precarious — it exists through executive action, not legislation, and provides no path to citizenship or permanent residency. But under the current administration, the erosion has accelerated. Starting last year, DHS officials began publicly urging DACA recipients to self-deport, arguing that the program "does not equate to automatically providing legal status."

The numbers bear out the shift. In a letter to senators earlier this year, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem disclosed that between January and November 2025, 261 DACA recipients were arrested and 86 were removed from the country. While those figures represent a small fraction of the total DACA population, they mark a sharp departure from the Obama and Biden administrations' treatment of Dreamers as categorically low-priority for enforcement.

A Pattern of Erosion

The BIA ruling is one piece of a broader strategy. The Department of Health and Human Services made DACA recipients ineligible for the federal healthcare marketplace last year. The Department of Education launched investigations into five universities that provide financial assistance to DACA recipients. And the administration has declined to issue regulations that would formally preserve the program, leaving it vulnerable to further legal challenges.

"For over a decade, DACA has endured relentless, politically motivated attacks," said Juliana Macedo do Nascimento of United We Dream, one of the largest immigrant youth organizations in the country.

The case also carried a notable political footnote: DHS had argued that the immigration judge in Santiago-Santiago should be recused because he is married to Democratic Representative Veronica Escobar of Texas, who has been outspoken on DACA issues. The BIA declined to rule on that argument, instead basing its decision on the legal merits.

What It Means Going Forward

For the half-million Dreamers who have built lives, careers, and families in the United States over the past fourteen years, the ruling adds another layer of vulnerability to an already fragile status. Any lapse in DACA renewal — whether due to processing delays, administrative error, or a future policy change — now carries the immediate risk of an active deportation case.

Immigration attorneys are advising DACA holders to explore any available pathway to a more permanent status, including family-based petitions and employer-sponsored visa applications. But for most Dreamers, no such pathway exists under current law.

Congress has repeatedly failed to pass legislation that would provide permanent protection. The DREAM Act, in various forms, has been introduced and stalled in every session since 2001. Without legislative action, DACA recipients remain subject to the shifting priorities of whichever administration holds power.
